extracted.intended_audience: comics fans, cartoonists, and researchers interested in newspaper comic craft and history
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit evaluative criteria for creating and preserving high-quality newspaper comic strips, focusing on artwork, storytelling, layout, themes, characterisation, and professional/ethical choices (e.g., merchandising, rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Artwork quality and ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Superb, rich illustrations with ambition and variety; revives artistic merits of classic comics and often uses breathtaking artwork (especially in Sunday color pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for dynamic artwork, strong composition, and technical skill; use distortion/exaggeration for effect. Watterson studied earlier masters (Winsor McCay, Herriman, Kelly, Schulz) and real-world references to make fantasy sequences believable. Avoid shrinking or overly simplifying artwork for economical printing; preserve detail where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual storytelling techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Use camera movements, varied poses and panel composition to convey motion and emotion (e.g., making a fall feel like slow-motion); sometimes rely on silent panels without dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make panels visually interesting even during conversation (e.g., showing movement on a wagon or sled). Use sequencing, composition and timing to deliver beats and emotional moments without depending solely on punchlines or text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layout and page design to preserve artwork
rubrics_metrics.description: Design pages and layouts so they survive newspaper cropping and preserve visual impact (Watterson changed layouts and placed speech balloons early to prevent editors cutting top panels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how editors may alter size; structure pages so critical imagery or flow isn't lost if panels are removed. When possible, negotiate for larger formats (half-page Sunday) to allow expressive artwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and experimentation in style and genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid routine by experimenting with different visual styles and subject-matter (science fiction, horror, film noir, realistic soap-opera styles, etc.) and by not settling on a single model for characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce occasional stylistic breaks and genre parodies to keep the strip fresh; vary tone and approach so readers are surprised rather than bored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative and fantasy sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the protagonist's imagination to create elaborate fantasy sequences (e.g., Spaceman Spiff, Stupendous Man) and transformations of ordinary objects (cardboard box becomes airplane/time machine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat fantasies as opportunities for different visuals and storytelling modes; research relevant details (e.g., paleontology for dinosaur fantasies) to make them convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional and philosophical depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Include thought-provoking life lessons and melancholy undertones alongside humor; strips can explore loneliness, death, fear, and meaningful observations about life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance humor with sincere moments that resonate emotionally; don't restrict the strip to gag-after-gag — occasional non-punchline, reflective strips can deepen reader attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Create multi-dimensional characters who can be both adorable and obnoxious; use character relationships (e.g., Hobbes as voice of reason) to reveal personality and to carry philosophical or humorous beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow characters to have consistent, distinctive voices and dynamics (private clubs, recurring gags), and use these to generate humor, conflict, and pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tackling serious themes and satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't shy away from addressing real-life issues (children's misbehavior, bullying, the environment, crime, death) and satirising cultural phenomena (television, commercialism, superhero comics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use satire thoughtfully and integrate social commentary into character-driven stories rather than turning strips into didactic pieces; juxtapose lighthearted play with sharper critiques when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding routine punchline dependency
rubrics_metrics.description: Move beyond always ending on a conventional punchline; sometimes a strip exists to move readers emotionally or philosophically rather than just to deliver a gag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow strips to land on quiet moments, rhetorical questions, or visual poetry — evaluate success by emotional effect and resonance, not only laugh frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-commercialism and protection of artistic integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist overexposure and merchandising that would cheapen the strip; maintain control over rights and presentation to keep the work's mystery and artistic value intact (Watterson refused merchandising and renegotiated rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider long-term artistic reputation when making licensing decisions; preserving scarcity and avoiding trivial merchandising can protect the strip’s perceived authenticity. Negotiating contractual control (rights, format) is a strategic tool for quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of presentation and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocate for favorable publication conditions (full half-page Sunday formats rather than reduced-size versions) to allow the artwork and experiments to be seen as intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with syndicates and editors toward publication formats that respect artistic composition; build contingencies (layout changes, speech balloon placement) if full format cannot be guaranteed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research-informed accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Inform imaginative sequences with factual research when necessary (e.g., reading paleontology books to depict dinosaurs correctly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subject-matter research to lend credibility to visual or narrative elements, improving reader immersion even in fantastical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career and production choices to preserve quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Make professional decisions (taking sabbaticals, retiring at peak, limiting publicity) that prioritize creative pace, reduce compromises, and protect the work's legacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate workload and commercial pressures; taking time off or ending a series deliberately can maintain standards and prevent dilution of artistic vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining mystery and selective public presence
rubrics_metrics.description: A reclusive or selective public profile (few interviews, limited photographs, occasional surreptitious gestures like hidden signed books) can contribute to a work's mystique and protect its reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how publicity choices affect reader perception and the mythology around a creator; measured absence can enhance focus on the work itself rather than celebrity.
